network.overall_strategy: Construct an anoxic surface network with 17 molecular species, 13 reaction nodes and 10 distinct reaction-sequence pathways. The best-supported target-forming chemistry is cyanoacetylene-derived 2-aminosuccinonitrile followed by competing hydrolysis to free asparagine and aspartate. The literature does not establish ten independent Asn-forming mechanisms: the ten pathways below distinguish feedstock-generation routes, maleonitrile versus fumaronitrile entrances, and a explicitly speculative cyanoacetaldehyde-recovery entrance. Shared chemistry is not counted as independent experimental confirmation. Hydrolysis is represented by net product branches rather than unsupported assignments of individual monoamide intermediates or hydrolysis order. Copper-mediated supply is conditional on a finite oxidized-copper inventory, without O2-dependent regeneration. Aspartate-to-asparagine amidation is omitted because no demonstrated prebiotic implementation is supplied. Numerical operating ranges are proposed screening and transport windows, not reported successful protocols or measured environmental concentrations. Capture efficiencies, intermediate survival, Asn/Asp branching and free-Asn loss rates remain unmeasured in these windows and must not be inferred from this graph. Reaction sequences are topological synthesis schedules: precursor-generation reactions can operate in separate compartments before their products merge. Formulas use neutral acid/base representatives except where explicit copper and proton charges are needed; actual aqueous protonation and ligand speciation depend on pH. Unspecified stereochemistry implies racemic products. The schema's intermediate role also covers connected coproducts and sinks.

reactions.name: HCN supply from methane–nitrogen discharge

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K bulk gas; non-equilibrium discharge excitation
conditions.other: Proposed local reducing-gas source: CH4:N2 molar ratio 1:1 to 1:10, without O2. Screen gas exposure times of 0.1-10 s with 1-24 h collection. Quench exiting gas into 300-310 K water within 1-10 s; receiver pH 9.5-10.0 favors cyanide retention. A captured total-cyanide concentration of 0.1-10 mM is an experimental input window, not a predicted yield. Measure gas-to-liquid recovery and volatilization losses.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical excitation generates carbon- and nitrogen-containing radicals that recombine into HCN within a complex product mixture. A balanced source projection is 2 CH4 + N2 -> 2 HCN + 3 H2; it is neither an elementary mechanism nor an exclusive product distribution.
reactions.reasoning: Discharge-derived nitrile feedstocks are consistent with Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and the discharge chemistry discussed by Shapiro (1999). These references do not establish an HCN yield or capture efficiency for the numerical window specified here. A methane-rich local plume is assumed rather than a globally strongly reducing atmosphere. This reaction and rxn_003 can coexist in one discharge mixture; separating their graph nodes describes product-specific source fluxes, not selective reactors.

reactions.name: Alternative HCN supply from methane–ammonia discharge

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K bulk gas; non-equilibrium discharge excitation
conditions.other: Proposed CH4:NH3 molar ratio 1:0.1 to 1:1, anoxic, with 0.1-10 s gas exposure and 1-24 h collection. Quench within 1-10 s into water at 300-310 K and pH 9.5-10.0. Screen captured total cyanide at 0.1-10 mM. Use a gas source separate from the cyanoacetylene generator; quantify NH3 carryover and prevent upstream gas back-mixing. Natural implementation of this separation remains unverified.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-driven dehydrogenation and radical chemistry yield HCN among other products. The balanced net source projection is CH4 + NH3 -> HCN + 3 H2.
reactions.reasoning: Reducing methane–ammonia discharge chemistry is supported at the mixture level by Johnson et al. (2008), while Shapiro (1999) discusses nitrile production and subsequent aqueous amino-acid chemistry. Johnson et al. did not identify Asn in the reanalyzed archive, so their results are not cited as direct Asn evidence. Spatial separation addresses the reported suppression of cyanoacetylene production by ammonia but does not establish successful feedstock delivery. The proposed mixture and transport windows require testing.

reactions.name: Cyanoacetylene supply from methane–nitrogen discharge

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K bulk gas; non-equilibrium discharge excitation
conditions.other: Proposed CH4:N2 molar ratio 1:1 to 1:10; exclude O2 and avoid NH3- or H2S-rich source gas. Screen 0.1-10 s gas exposure, followed by quenching within 1-10 s into a 300-310 K receiver. Test captured cyanoacetylene at 0.05-5 mM and delivery to cyanide addition within 1-10 min. These are transport targets, not measured survival times. An optically attenuated receiver limits additional surface photochemistry.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge fragmentation and radical recombination assemble the unsaturated C3 nitrile. A balanced source projection is 6 CH4 + N2 -> 2 C3HN + 11 H2; substantial coproduct chemistry is omitted from this target-focused projection.
reactions.reasoning: Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) explicitly identified cyanoacetylene as a major nitrogen-containing discharge product from methane and nitrogen. Shapiro (1999) cautioned that ammonia or hydrogen sulfide suppresses its production. The separated source therefore has chemical motivation, but capture, dilution, receiver chemistry and transfer survival remain unresolved. Neither the balanced projection nor the proposed residence times imply an experimental yield.

reactions.name: Conditional O2-free copper-mediated oxidative cyanation of acetylene
agents: Cu(I)-cyanide complexes as coupling promoters; Cu(II) is a consumed oxidant

conditions.other: Conditional screening window: initial pH 8.5-9.5; dissolved acetylene 0.1-1 mM; total cyanide 1-10 mM; Cu(II) inventory 0.2-2 mM; initiating Cu(I) inventory 0.01-0.1 mM; 1 min-6 h. No O2 or oxidant regeneration is assumed. Proton production consumes finite alkalinity, so pH drift must be recorded. Requires a transient sulfide-poor microenvironment isolated from Fe(II)-rich fluids; its geological availability is unverified. Transfer product to the addition stage within 1-10 min as a test target.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-associated acetylene and cyanide undergo oxidative C-C coupling. Explicit redox bookkeeping for the proposed anoxic implementation is C2H2 + HCN + 2 Cu(II) -> C3HN + 2 Cu(I) + 2 H+. Copper ligand speciation and elementary coupling steps are unresolved in this coarse representation.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support copper-promoted acetylene–HCN coupling as a cyanoacetylene source. The finite-Cu(II), O2-free implementation and numerical conditions encoded here are conditional extrapolations, not a demonstrated continuously operating geochemical system. Cu(II) reduction by abundant Fe(II), copper precipitation by sulfide and cyanide side oxidation are serious competitors. Cu(II) is therefore represented as a consumed molecular input, not hidden as a catalyst. If a suitable oxidized-copper inventory cannot be established, pathways P5-P8 are unavailable.

reactions.name: Maleonitrile-forming branch of cyanoacetylene hydrocyanation

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.0-10.0; cyanoacetylene 0.05-5 mM; total HCN/CN 1-50 mM; sampling after 10 min, 1 h, 6 h and 24 h. Use anoxic, optically attenuated water in a shaded pool or rock pore. Quantify both alkene geometries and cyanoacetaldehyde. The same window applies to rxn_006; no selective production of the Z isomer is asserted.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the activated alkyne, followed by proton transfer to give the Z unsaturated dinitrile branch.
reactions.reasoning: The cyanoacetylene–HCN–ammonia entrance to the Asn/Asp precursor family is supported by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Patel et al. (2015). The supplied findings identify maleonitrile/fumaronitrile chemistry but do not establish a controllable E/Z ratio, substrate-specific rate constants or a superior geometry. This node represents one product branch, not a demonstrated stereoselective preparation. Its numerical screening conditions are proposed.

reactions.name: Fumaronitrile-forming branch of cyanoacetylene hydrocyanation

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.0-10.0; cyanoacetylene 0.05-5 mM; total HCN/CN 1-50 mM; sampling after 10 min, 1 h, 6 h and 24 h. Anoxic, optically attenuated aqueous setting. Measure the E/Z product distribution rather than assigning separate favorable conditions to the two geometries.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition and proton transfer produce the E unsaturated dinitrile branch. This net node does not resolve whether geometry is established during addition or subsequent isomerization.
reactions.reasoning: Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Patel et al. (2015) support the overall nitrile precursor chemistry summarized in the supplied findings. They do not, in that evidence summary, establish the elementary origin or productive flux of each geometry separately. Fumaronitrile is consequently a chemically distinct entrance without an asserted performance advantage over maleonitrile.

reactions.name: Ammonia addition to maleonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.0-10.5; maleonitrile 0.01-5 mM; total NH3/NH4 10-100 mM; time points 1, 6, 24 and 72 h. Use low-gas-exchange, optically attenuated pores or covered pools; ammonia volatilization must be measured. Transfer newly formed aminodinitrile to a separately characterized hydrolysis aliquot rather than assuming long-term storage stability.

reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia across the electron-poor C=C bond, followed by proton transfer, produces 2-aminosuccinonitrile without an expected prebiotic enantioselective bias.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identify the Asn/Asp aminonitrile precursor branch, building on the cyanoacetylene chemistry of Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966). Addition to an activated unsaturated dinitrile is chemically consistent with that branch. The supplied evidence does not quantify the isolated maleonitrile conversion or aminodinitrile lifetime under these proposed conditions; ammonia addition must outcompete other dinitrile reactions.

reactions.name: Ammonia addition to fumaronitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.0-10.5; fumaronitrile 0.01-5 mM; total NH3/NH4 10-100 mM; time points 1, 6, 24 and 72 h. Anoxic and optically attenuated, with low gas exchange. Compare conversion and aminodinitrile survival directly with rxn_007; equal yields or equal rates are not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds across the activated alkene and proton transfer yields the same saturated 2-aminosuccinonitrile connectivity reached from maleonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The common precursor chemistry is supported at the reaction-family level by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Patel et al. (2015). Saturation removes the starting alkene geometry, justifying convergence on one molecular node. The numerical window and geometry-specific kinetics remain unvalidated; this entrance does not independently validate downstream Asn formation.

reactions.name: Competing hydration of cyanoacetylene to cyanoacetaldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed competition screen: pH 6.0-9.0; cyanoacetylene 0.05-5 mM; initially low added cyanide and ammonia; sampling after 1 min, 10 min, 1 h, 6 h and 24 h. Maintain anoxia and optical attenuation. Compare directly with cyanide-rich receivers to determine whether capture into rxn_005/rxn_006 outruns hydration. The aldehyde's subsequent lifetime is not known.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to the activated alkyne followed by proton transfers and tautomerization gives cyanoacetaldehyde. Water is both reagent and solvent; no selective mineral catalyst is assigned.
reactions.reasoning: Shapiro (1999) identifies cyanoacetylene hydrolysis to cyanoacetaldehyde as an important competing process. This is therefore included even though it can drain the better-supported dinitrile entrance. The proposed numerical window is not a reported rate law. Whether the resulting aldehyde is a recoverable intermediate rather than an effective loss depends on the speculative rxn_010 and on competing aldehyde chemistry.

reactions.name: Speculative Strecker recovery of cyanoacetaldehyde

conditions.other: Hypothesis-testing window: pH 8.0-9.5; freshly generated cyanoacetaldehyde 0.01-2 mM; total cyanide 1-20 mM; total NH3/NH4 10-100 mM; time points 10 min, 1 h, 6 h and 24 h. Begin capture within 1-10 min of aldehyde formation as a test target. Quantify carbonyl side products, reversible cyanohydrin formation and aminodinitrile recovery. No productive residence-time window has been established.

reactions.mechanism: The aldehyde condenses reversibly with ammonia to an imine/iminium species; cyanide capture gives NC-CH2-CH(NH2)-CN, with net water elimination.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate and prebiotic setting: the supplied research does not demonstrate productive Strecker capture of cyanoacetaldehyde. Shapiro (1999) supports its formation as a cyanoacetylene sink, while Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Patel et al. (2015) support the destination precursor family, not this connecting reaction. The proposal is justified by the aldehyde functionality and correct Strecker carbon accounting, but aldehyde survival and productive flux must be established before P9 or P10 can be called demonstrated routes.

reactions.name: Net Asn-forming branch of aminodinitrile hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions in acidic screening arms
Hydroxide ions in alkaline screening arms

conditions.temperature: 300-360 K, with separate tests at 300, 323 and 353 K
conditions.catalyst: Acid/base catalysis where applicable; no assigned mineral selectivity
conditions.other: Unvalidated screening matrix, not an established synthesis window: initial aminodinitrile 0.1-10 mM; separate pH 2, 4, 7, 9 and 10 aliquots; sample after 0.5, 2, 6, 24 and 72 h. No added acid/base catalyst in the neutral arm. Measure Asn, Asp, residual nitriles and positional amide products. Rapidly cool analytical aliquots to 300 K or below and adjust to pH 6-7 without prolonged hydrolysis. Use non-hydrolytic analysis, authentic standards and orthogonal identification; do not use 6 M HCl workup. No yield or branching fraction is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved multistep hydration/hydrolysis converts the alpha nitrile to a carboxyl group while the side-chain nitrile reaches the amide oxidation state. The net balance is C4H5N3 + 3 H2O -> C4H8N2O3 + NH3. This is an endpoint branch, not a specified monoamide sequence or a claim that hydrolysis stops selectively.
reactions.reasoning: Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) support free Asn formation alongside Asp in the overall cyanoacetylene chemistry. Patel et al. (2015) support the aminodinitrile precursor branch, not a selective Asn yield or resolved hydration order. Accordingly, experimental support is at the overall route-family level; the proposed numerical matrix and isolated-precursor branching remain unverified. This is the decisive bottleneck: a measurable free-Asn fraction must form before competing hydrolysis and subsequent loss. Resolving this net node into assumed alpha-first or side-chain-first intermediates would overstate the available evidence.

reactions.name: Competing net full hydrolysis of aminodinitrile to aspartate
agents: Hydronium ions in acidic screening arms
Hydroxide ions in alkaline screening arms

conditions.other: Use the same 0.1-10 mM precursor concentration, pH 2, 4, 7, 9 and 10 aliquots, and 0.5-72 h sampling schedule as rxn_011. Extend selected time courses to 7 days to examine over-hydrolysis. Determine Asp formation together with free-Asn loss rather than treating endpoint Asp as proof that no Asn ever formed. Optically attenuated, anoxic aqueous conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Both nitrile groups ultimately become carboxyl groups, releasing ammonia. The net balance is C4H5N3 + 4 H2O -> C4H7NO4 + 2 NH3. This endpoint channel lumps routes to Asp that do not accumulate a measurable free-Asn pool.
reactions.reasoning: Mixed Asp/Asn production is supported by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966), and the common precursor assignment is supported by Patel et al. (2015). No selective amide-preserving window is established in the supplied research. This node is needed to represent the competing acid endpoint, but its flux is unknown. In kinetic fitting it must be distinguished from the explicitly resolved Asn-to-Asp flux in rxn_013; endpoint yields alone cannot identify both rates.

reactions.name: Loss of free asparagine by side-chain amide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Proposed free-Asn stability measurements: Asn 0.01-5 mM; pH 2, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10; time points from 0.5 h to 30 days. Include a 300-305 K, pH 6-7 retention arm after precursor hydrolysis. Use anoxic, optically attenuated solutions and non-hydrolytic analysis. No free-Asn half-life is assigned. Additional thermal decomposition products outside this hydrolysis channel must be checked experimentally.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the side-chain amide carbonyl and subsequent proton transfers release ammonia, giving the net reaction Asn + H2O -> Asp + NH3. This node concerns free Asn and does not invoke a peptide-backbone succinimide mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Free-amide hydrolysis is a chemically established loss process, but the supplied literature does not provide a calibrated free-Asn rate law over this proposed window. Vallentyne (1964) provides relevant thermal-stability context. Geiger and Clarke (1987) studied peptide-bound Asn, so their reported half-life is explicitly not transferred to free Asn. Weiss et al. (2018) examined much hotter solid-state decomposition and likewise does not calibrate this aqueous reaction. Direct formation-versus-loss measurements are required to establish accumulation.

pathways.name: Nitrogen-derived HCN, discharge cyanoacetylene, maleonitrile entrance
pathways.description: Generate HCN and cyanoacetylene from methane–nitrogen discharge source fluxes, capture the Z dinitrile branch, add ammonia and access the net mixed-hydrolysis Asn branch. This is a representative best-supported route-family candidate, not a demonstrated optimum. Capture efficiency and the numerical Asn-production window remain unverified.

pathways.name: Nitrogen-derived HCN, discharge cyanoacetylene, fumaronitrile entrance
pathways.description: Use the methane–nitrogen source fluxes and the E dinitrile entrance before convergence on aminodinitrile hydrolysis. The geometry distinguishes this sequence from P1 but does not establish a different yield or independent target-forming mechanism.

pathways.name: Ammonia-derived HCN, separate discharge cyanoacetylene, maleonitrile entrance
pathways.description: Supply HCN from a methane–ammonia discharge while generating cyanoacetylene separately from methane and nitrogen. Merge captured products for the maleonitrile entrance. Source separation is motivated by ammonia suppression of cyanoacetylene production, but its natural implementation and recovery performance are not established.

pathways.name: Ammonia-derived HCN, separate discharge cyanoacetylene, fumaronitrile entrance
pathways.description: Combine the separated methane–ammonia HCN source with methane–nitrogen cyanoacetylene generation and the fumaronitrile entrance. The same unresolved capture, aminodinitrile hydrolysis and free-Asn survival constraints apply as in P3.

pathways.name: Nitrogen-derived HCN, conditional copper supply, maleonitrile entrance
pathways.description: Use methane–nitrogen-derived HCN both for acetylene cyanation and subsequent dinitrile formation. Proceed through maleonitrile and the shared Asn-forming endpoint branch. Conditional on rxn_004: a finite Cu(II) inventory and protection from Fe(II)/sulfide consumption are required; O2 regeneration is not allowed or assumed.

pathways.name: Nitrogen-derived HCN, conditional copper supply, fumaronitrile entrance
pathways.description: Follow copper-mediated cyanoacetylene supply with the fumaronitrile entrance. This is a distinct reaction sequence but not independent evidence for Asn hydrolysis kinetics. It is unavailable if the conditional anoxic copper source cannot operate.

pathways.name: Ammonia-derived HCN, conditional copper supply, maleonitrile entrance
pathways.description: Feed methane–ammonia-derived HCN to the finite-oxidant copper cyanation branch, then proceed through maleonitrile. HCN supply provenance differs from P5, while the copper feasibility and downstream hydrolysis limitations are shared.

pathways.name: Ammonia-derived HCN, conditional copper supply, fumaronitrile entrance
pathways.description: Use the methane–ammonia HCN source, conditional copper-mediated cyanoacetylene formation and the E dinitrile entrance. This candidate does not establish either a naturally sustained copper redox cycle or a measured free-Asn accumulation window.

pathways.name: Nitrogen-derived HCN with speculative cyanoacetaldehyde recovery
pathways.description: Generate HCN and cyanoacetylene by methane–nitrogen discharge, allow the documented aldehyde-forming hydration branch, and test recovery through Strecker chemistry before aminodinitrile hydrolysis. This is an explicitly speculative synthesis route because productive rxn_010 and aldehyde survival are not demonstrated.

pathways.name: Ammonia-derived HCN with speculative cyanoacetaldehyde recovery
pathways.description: Supply HCN from a separate methane–ammonia discharge and cyanoacetylene from methane–nitrogen discharge, then test aldehyde hydration and Strecker recovery. This differs from P9 in HCN supply but retains the same unverified aldehyde-capture step and shared Asn-production bottleneck.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A coherent route through the literature-supported aminodinitrile chemistry of Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Patel et al. (2015). The discharge equations are valid net formation summaries, not elementary mechanisms. Free-Asn formation has experimental precedent, but rxn_011 does not establish a productive hydrolysis window or Asn/Asp partition under the proposed surface conditions.
suggestions: Specify discharge composition, aqueous pH and temperature, and gas-to-liquid capture conditions and residence times.
Measure aminodinitrile conversion, free Asn, Asp and subsequent Asn loss using an analytical method that does not first hydrolyze Asn.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The fumaronitrile entrance gives the correct aminodinitrile connectivity and a plausible route to Asn. The supplied literature supports this reaction family, but does not establish separate environmental performance for each geometric-isomer branch. There is no supplied basis for ranking this entrance above or below P1. The principal shared uncertainty remains productive partial hydrolysis.
suggestions: Measure the maleonitrile/fumaronitrile product distribution and isomer-specific ammonia-addition kinetics.
Supply reaction-linked experimental references and determine the hydrolysis residence time that permits detectable free Asn.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Generating HCN separately from cyanoacetylene is chemically coherent and addresses the ammonia-related suppression of cyanoacetylene production discussed by Shapiro (1999). The downstream maleonitrile route has the same evidentiary support as P1. Compartment separation is proposed, but capture efficiencies, transfer times and the final hydrolysis conditions are not supplied.
suggestions: Specify how the ammonia-containing HCN source remains separate from the cyanoacetylene-producing discharge until aqueous capture.
Measure precursor delivery and survival together with Asn/Asp branching rather than assuming that independently generated precursors merge quantitatively.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a valid synthesis schedule using separately generated precursors and the fumaronitrile entrance. Neither the alternative HCN source nor the geometric-isomer branch introduces a conservation or connectivity defect. Its target-forming chemistry remains the same experimentally supported but environmentally unquantified aminodinitrile hydrolysis used by P1-P3.
suggestions: Define aqueous mixing conditions that provide sufficient reactive cyanide and ammonia while accounting for precursor losses.
Measure fumaronitrile conversion and free-Asn formation in the actual combined precursor mixture, not only with purified starting materials.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The copper equation conserves atoms and charge with two Cu(II) ions consumed per cyanoacetylene, so molecular oxygen is not required by its net stoichiometry. Patel et al. (2015) support related copper-mediated chemistry, but the supplied evidence does not establish performance of this exact finite-inventory formulation. Copper speciation and productive coupling remain additional uncertainties beyond the shared hydrolysis bottleneck.
suggestions: Document or test the exact oxygen-free coupling conditions, including copper oxidation states, ligands, precipitation and cyanoacetylene release.
Specify the finite oxidized-copper inventory and budget HCN for both oxidative cyanation and subsequent hydrocyanation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The fumaronitrile branch is chemically coherent, but its precursor supply remains conditional on productive rxn_004. A finite Cu(II) inventory is internally compatible with anoxia; it is not equivalent to demonstrated catalytic turnover. Cyanide coordination and competing copper reactions require assessment under the actual coupling conditions. No conservation violation is present.
suggestions: Measure cyanoacetylene production per equivalent of Cu(II), including cyanide and copper material balances.
Test whether the coupling mixture can feed fumaronitrile formation and ammonia addition without an unsupported purification or transfer assumption.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The ammonia-derived HCN supply is plausible and connects correctly to the copper-mediated entrance. Its success nevertheless depends on the unverified operating details of rxn_004 and the shared Asn-producing hydrolysis. If material from the HCN-generation compartment is transferred directly, ammonia carryover can alter copper coordination and must be included in the compatibility assessment.
suggestions: Quantify HCN capture and any ammonia carryover, then test their effects on copper speciation and coupling yield.
Establish downstream aminodinitrile and free-Asn yields using the resulting coupling mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This schedule is topologically valid and has no atom or charge imbalance. The alternative HCN source and fumaronitrile entrance do not resolve the conditional copper supply or establish a hydrolysis window for retaining the side-chain amide. The exact oxygen-free copper formulation needs reaction-level experimental support before this complete route can be regarded as established.
suggestions: Specify coupling pH, temperature, copper inventory and ligand composition, with a reference supporting those conditions.
Measure the fumaronitrile-to-aminodinitrile conversion and subsequent Asn/Asp distribution in the copper-containing product stream.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanoacetylene hydration is a supported competing process. Strecker chemistry of cyanoacetaldehyde would give the correct 2-aminosuccinonitrile connectivity and is balanced, but the supplied research does not demonstrate this recovery reaction under the proposed conditions. Explicitly labeling rxn_010 speculative is appropriate; it does not establish that hydration becomes a productive entrance rather than a net sink.
suggestions: Test cyanoacetaldehyde with HCN and ammonia and directly identify 2-aminosuccinonitrile before hydrolysis.
Measure recovery yield against competing cyanoacetaldehyde reactions, then quantify free-Asn production from the recovered material.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Separate ammonia-derived HCN and methane-nitrogen cyanoacetylene production are a coherent precursor schedule. The subsequent recovery entrance remains a chemically plausible but experimentally unverified Strecker proposal. Asn formation therefore depends on both successful rxn_010 and the same unresolved hydrolysis partition governing the other pathways; the alternative HCN source supplies no additional evidence for either step.
suggestions: Define the transfer and mixing conditions for independently generated HCN and cyanoacetaldehyde.
Validate rxn_010 in the relevant precursor mixture and measure free-Asn formation and loss without relying on peptide-bound Asn deamidation rates.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is connected, has sufficient molecule and reaction nodes, and uses molecule IDs consistently. The deterministic balance check establishes that all 13 reactions conserve atoms and charge with appropriate coefficients; none is a conservation violation. The inferred coefficients are reasonable and should be recorded explicitly. Connected coproducts and sinks are legitimate network components. P1-P4 are equally supported here, with P1 selected as a representative best pathway. The aminodinitrile route has experimental precedent for free Asn alongside Asp, and the network appropriately avoids claiming selective Asn production, an established hydrolysis order, or demonstrated Asp-to-Asn amidation. Reactions rxn_012 and rxn_013 are chemically reasonable competing hydrolysis and product-loss processes. Their rates and the branching through rxn_011 remain unmeasured; no rapid free-Asn loss rate can be inferred from peptide deamidation data. Environmental validation is incomplete: despite mentioning proposed numerical windows, the submission supplies no actual reaction-level temperature, pressure, pH or residence-time ranges, and compartment separation lacks quantitative capture and transfer details. The finite-Cu(II) assumption makes rxn_004 stoichiometrically compatible with anoxia, but its exact operating chemistry and inventory require support. Reaction rxn_010 remains a plausible, explicitly speculative recovery option. These optional branches do not invalidate the discharge-fed core. Literature alignment is strong conceptually, especially in acknowledging supply fragility and uncontrolled Asn/Asp partitioning, but reaction-linked citations and supporting protocols are missing. The ten schedules are not treated as ten independent experimental demonstrations. Listed problematic reactions denote evidentiary or operational gaps, not imbalance. Overall, this is a credible network proposal whose integrated target production remains insufficiently validated for approval at the 0.90 network threshold.
